span.label: mechanism
span.quote: As figure – ground modulations depend on feedback from extrastriate areas, these results suggest that masking selectively interrupts the recurrent interactions between V1 and higher visual areas.

span.label: backward masking of figure–ground segregation
span.quote: In a backward masking paradigm, a target stimulus is rapidly (<100 msec) followed by a second stimulus.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: Meanwhile, we recorded neural activity from neurons in V1 (Figure 2).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The mask replaces the target's information at the low level by the time descending signals arrive, so the recurrent V1-extrastriate loop that generates figure-ground modulation is cut off while the feedforward sweep is left intact.
span.quote: As figure – ground modulations depend on feedback from extrastriate areas, these results suggest that masking selectively interrupts the recurrent interactions between V1 and higher visual areas.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Perception proceeds in stages: a feedforward sweep first analyses elementary features, then recurrent interactions between V1 and higher areas bind them into a coherent percept, and only when that recurrent activity spreads into executive areas can a conscious report be made.
span.quote: Early on, feedforward processing analyzes the scene in terms of its elementary features. Next, recurrent processing, involving widespread interactions between visual areas including V1 and higher areas, lays the foundations for a coherent percept of the

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Figure-ground modulation is necessary but not sufficient for report, because an independent decision stage is interposed between the V1 modulation and the animal's behavioural response.
span.quote: When there is no modulation, there is no perception. However, when there is modulation, this does not in itself guarantee that the animal ‘‘reports’’ to have seen the stimulus. A decision process sits between the modulation and the animals report, which is independent of the modulation.

span.label: Orientation selectivity at the multiunit recording sites was weak, limiting the sensitivity of the feature-signal measure.

span.label: The texture orientation comparison used only two fixed orientations, which further weakened the measured selectivity.
span.quote: For the orientation of texture elements, the selectivity is even less pronounced, in part because there were only two orientations, fixed at 458 and 1358, to compare.

span.label: The conclusion is one inferential step from the measurement, and the premise is stated.

We show that the V1 figure – ground signals are selectively and fully suppressed at target – mask intervals that psychophysically result in the target being invisible. Initial response transients, signalling the features that make up the scene, are not affected

span.label: Feedforward inhibitory models
span.quote: Feedforward inhibitory models explain backward masking by asserting that the second stimulus exerts an inhibitory influence on the neural signal that is evoked by the first stimulus. This inhibition is postulated to occur at levels of processing before stimuli are fully categorized and made available to conscious recognition systems. In other words, the second stimulus somehow catches up with the first one before it reaches a conscious level (Breitmeyer, 1984). Another type of models argues that masking interferes with socalled reentrant or recurrent processing

span.label: the masking effect - SELECTIVE, AND BOTH HALVES ARE IN ONE SENTENCE: figure-ground signals are fully suppressed at exactly the intervals that make the target invisible, while the initial response transients are not affected, so 'masking reduces responses in V1' names one of two opposite results

span.label: the conclusion - HELD GIVEN AN IMPORTED PREMISE: the measurement is a suppression in V1 and the conclusion is about recurrent interactions with higher areas, reached because figure-ground modulations are taken to depend on feedback from extrastriate areas, and offered as a suggestion
span.quote: As figure – ground modulations depend on feedback from extrastriate areas, these results suggest that masking selectively interrupts the recurrent interactions between V1 and higher visual areas

span.label: backward masking - TWO RIVAL MODEL FAMILIES, NAMED: feedforward inhibitory models have the second stimulus inhibiting the first before it reaches a conscious level, while another family has masking interfering with reentrant or recurrent processing; the same phenomenon supports two different accounts of where it happens

span.label: t-test
span.quote: Significant modulation ( p < .025) is only found at SOAs of 5, 6, 7, and 8 frames (two-sided t test with the electrodes as a group, t statistics for the 1- to 8-frame conditions: 0.40, 0.13, 0.44, 2.23, 5.21, 4.96, 5.96, 3.17, respectively).

span.label: t-test
span.quote: significant differences between optimal and suboptimal texture orientations can be observed at all SOAs except 1 frame (Figure 6 top) (one-sided t test with the electrodes as a group, t statistics for the 1- to 8-frame conditions: 0.38, 1.83, 2.59, 3.37, 2.66, 4.21, 3.56, 4.04, respectively).

span.label: p-value
span.quote: Significant ( p < .025) modulation is found at all SOAs except that of 1 frame (Figure 5 bottom)

span.quote: The mean squared difference between these two measures is 0.033.

span.label: median
span.quote: The median orientation selectivity ratio (average response level while a bar of optimal orientation moved over the RF divided by average response for least effective orientation) was 1.94 (mean = 2.19, range = 1.16 – 9.03).

span.label: normalization
span.quote: Therefore, we normalized at each electrode all responses obtained for all stimulus conditions to the maximum response obtained at that electrode.

span.label: Backward masking abolishes the figure-ground signal in V1 exactly at those target-mask intervals at which the monkey cannot see the figure.
span.quote: We show that the V1 figure – ground signals are selectively and fully suppressed at target – mask intervals that psychophysically result in the target being invisible.

span.label: The early transient V1 response that codes the local features of the scene survives the mask untouched.
span.quote: Initial response transients, signalling the features that make up the scene, are not affected.

span.label: With a texture pattern mask at short SOAs the monkeys performed at chance in locating the figure, confirming that the masks made the figure invisible.
span.quote: When the figure – ground stimuli were followed by the texture pattern masks, at short SOAs, the monkeys were at chance in detecting the position of the figures.

span.label: When the same brief displays were followed by a blank screen instead of a mask, figure-ground modulation remained present even at the shortest SOAs, so the suppression is caused by the mask and not by the short presentation.
span.quote: We found that figure – ground signals are still present at very short SOAs (Figure 5 top).

span.label: Orientation selectivity for the texture elements was essentially unaffected by backward masking at every SOA but the shortest.
span.quote: Orientation selectivity for texture elements (Figure 6 bottom) is hardly affected by backward masking (except at an SOA of 1 frame).

span.label: Orientation information about the line segments remains available in V1 even at the SOAs at which the animals see nothing.
span.quote: Our results show that information about the orientation of the line segments is available in V1 at even the shortest SOAs (2 and 3 frames).

span.label: The neurometric curve of figure-ground modulation tracks the behavioural psychometric curve far better (error 0.033) than the neurometric curve of orientation selectivity does (error 0.138), which rules out a purely feedforward account of figure-ground segregation.
span.quote: we found a much worse correspondence (mean squared error = 0.138) than when the same psychometric curve is compared with the neurometric curve of figure – ground modulation (where the error is 0.033, Figure 4 bottom).

span.label: Trial by trial, the amount of figure-ground modulation did not predict whether the monkey reported seeing the figure.
span.quote: We analyzed our data to determine whether there was a trial by trial relation between the monkeys report on the visibility of the figure (indicated by the eye movement) and the amount of figure – ground modulation (in the neural data). We did not find any significant effect (data not shown).

span.label: Detection of the figure occurs only when the stimulus also drives recurrent processing between V1 and higher areas, expressed as figure-ground modulation of V1 activity.
span.quote: Only when the stimulus also engages recurrent processing between high and low cortical areas, which results in figure – ground modulation of V1 activity, the animal is able to detect it.

span.label: backward masking
span.quote: When a visual stimulus is rapidly followed by another one, the visibility of the first stimulus may be greatly reduced, depending on factors like relative timing (stimulus onset asynchrony [SOA]), similarity, and spatial position of the two stimuli (Enns & DiLollo, 2000; Breitmeyer, 1984). This phenomenon is known as backward masking.

span.label: recurrent (reentrant) processing
span.quote: processing, information flows from low to high levels, and then back again to the low levels (and this may occur several times).

span.label: figure-ground modulation
span.quote: Figure – ground modulation is the difference between neural activity evoked by texture elements that belong to a figure and activity evoked by the same elements of

span.label: feedforward inhibitory model of masking
span.quote: Feedforward inhibitory models explain backward masking by asserting that the second stimulus exerts an inhibitory influence on the neural signal that is evoked by the first stimulus.

span.quote: The stimuli were presented for variable durations, ranging from 1 monitor frame (14 msec) to 8 monitor frames (110 msec). Subsequently, a mask was presented.

span.term: type of second stimulus (texture pattern mask vs. blank screen)
span.quote: In a separate set of experiments, the stimuli were not followed by these pattern masks, but simply by a blank screen of approximately equal mean luminance as the textured figure – ground scene.

span.label: figure position (left or right of fixation, i.e. figure vs. background on the receptive field)
span.term: figure position (left or right of fixation, i.e. figure vs. background on the receptive field)
span.quote: The square figure was positioned either to the right or the left of the fixation spot, so that in one of these two positions, the figure covered the RFs of the neurons that we recorded from.

span.quote: To quantify the amount of modulation at the different SOAs, we calculated, per recording site, the mean level of activity evoked by the two sets of stimuli during the 40-msec interval where modulation is to be expected

span.quote: Top: Percentage correct responses (i.e., saccades towards the figure position), with respect to SOA between figure – ground display and pattern mask, for the two animals O and P.

span.term: orientation selectivity of the V1 response
span.quote: we quantified the amount of orientation selectivity by taking the mean response levels during a 40-msec interval starting at 50 msec after stimulus onset (dotted line in Figure 6 top).

span.label: local stimulus content of the receptive field, held identical across the compared figure and ground conditions
span.term: local stimulus content of the receptive field, held identical across the compared figure and ground conditions
span.quote: From the point of view of what is on the receptive field (RF), the two sets of stimuli are identical.

span.label: mask identity, equated across the four stimulus types by blocking
span.term: mask identity, equated across the four stimulus types by blocking
span.quote: All trials were blocked in such a way that all four stimulus types (A – D) were equally often followed by any of the 12 mask types.

span.label: 0.033 — mean squared difference between the figure-ground neurometric curve and the behavioural psychometric curve
span.quote: The mean squared difference between these two measures is 0.033.

span.label: 0.138 — mean squared error between the orientation-selectivity neurometric curve and the same psychometric curve, i.e. the much poorer feedforward fit
span.quote: we found a much worse correspondence (mean squared error = 0.138) than when the same psychometric curve is compared with the neurometric curve of figure – ground modulation (where the error is 0.033, Figure 4 bottom).

span.label: p < .025 — significance threshold at which figure-ground modulation was present only at SOAs of 5-8 frames under pattern masking
span.quote: Significant modulation ( p < .025) is only found at SOAs of 5, 6, 7, and 8 frames (two-sided t test with the electrodes as a group, t statistics for the 1- to 8-frame conditions: 0.40, 0.13, 0.44, 2.23, 5.21, 4.96, 5.96, 3.17, respectively).

span.label: 25 of these 32 electrodes — number of implanted V1 recording channels contributing data to this study
span.quote: For the present experiments, we recorded from 25 of these 32 electrodes in total, selected on the basis of RF position and the presence of contextual modulation.

span.label: 700 (total 11,000) — trials collected per SOA/mask condition, and in total, for the neural analysis
span.quote: about 700 trials (total 11,000) of neural data were collected

span.label: 1.94 — median orientation-selectivity ratio of the multiunit recording sites
span.quote: The median orientation selectivity ratio (average response level while a bar of optimal orientation moved over the RF divided by average response for least effective orientation) was 1.94 (mean = 2.19, range = 1.16 – 9.03).

span.label: 14 – 110 msec — range of stimulus-onset asynchronies (1 to 8 monitor frames) between figure-ground display and mask
span.quote: These displays were shown for 1 to 8 monitor frames (14 – 110 msec) and were then followed by a texture pattern mask.

span.label: 100 msec — latency at which V1 responses start to distinguish figure from background texture
span.quote: responses to the figure texture are stronger than to background texture, starting at a latency of 100 msec, indicating that at this latency, neurons signal figure – ground relationships.

span.label: 0.18 — maximum figure-ground modulation, equated to 100% correct when building the neurometric curve
span.quote: we took the maximum amount of modulation (0.18) and equated this to 100% correct performance
